Today an agreement was reached over the economic well-being of Indonesia. With increases in foreign trade potential due to recent agreements, the potential for revenue and development is growing.

Opposition parties have reached across the aisle to PDI-P to commit to economic development plans. Opposition parties and PKB seem to be having a lot of say in the matter, insiders think that this may be in exchange for going along more with PDI-P's current liberalization policies.

Although a fully modernized Indonesia is many years off, the current government believes that the current plan will balance the immediate needs of the nation and its future needs. Work is to be done to expand Indonesian infrastructure in rural regions and improve education, among other things.

To help finance these plans, barriers to private companies abroad have been lowered in hopes that they will come to and invest in Indonesia, providing income from taxation as well as growing the economy and helping to raise the standard of living. Many groups within the legislature were not happy at this idea, but it was decided to be an easy way to help stimulate growth for both short and long term. Indonesia also plans to raise exports, and try to grow local markets to make Indonesia more self-sustaining.

The economic plans are expected to increase revenues and expenditures. For now the ratio is expected to stay much the same, but private investors and companies may further stimulate growth. However, only time will tell just what effect the plans will have.

The plans have met with a mildly positive reception within the nation. Abroad, Moody's is positive about it, and is considering raising Indonesia's credit rating to Baaa2

The government also expressed its support to social organizations within the country who are helping to provide support for the needy.

"I applaud the social organizations that are helping to keep us together," noted President Joko Widodo, "and I believe that they are also capable of preserving moral uprightness in our people in ways that governance cannot."

Some indicate that the President's comment may indicate further shifts from morality being politically enforced.
